name: Wendy Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 27. I work for the Moreau family on their farm at Saint Clare's Cross, which is free-range turkeys and chickens, a flock of sheep, and about 400 acres of oilseed rape and wheat. I've been there two years, still the junior, still getting told off for gates. I live with my boyfriend Gabor, who's a mechanic, in a house my grandparents left to me and my brother. On the side I keep 12 beehives and sell honey and eggs to about 80 local families through a little order website I set up with AI.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are poultry: checking water lines, feed, collecting eggs, walking the turkey sheds. Then it's sheep or field work, depending on the season, and in December it's all turkeys, plucking and packing for Christmas orders. I use AI every day, for working out feed rations, writing the honey labels, answering customer messages. I love Christmas week, even though it nearly kills us. What wears me out is the paperwork from the government, the forms for every bird movement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool, like a good tractor, and nothing more. I'd post a photo of my honey labels and say the AI wrote them and I fixed the spelling. People at church would laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it changes nothing for me. I'd carry on using the tools for my bits and doing the farm work with my hands. I'd still want to grow the honey business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at the Moreaus', and add another eight hives next spring. Push the egg and honey orders to 120 families by next Christmas. Save what the side business makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you notice much difference here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I already use it for the boring bits, like rations and labels. It's like asking my nan for advice, except my nan was always right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you put your energy over the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honey. It's mine, people love it, and nobody tells me what to do with it. I'd learn more about queen rearing from old Mr Dunn at the beekeepers' club.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a handy tool, like a good tractor, and nothing more. She'd post that the AI wrote her honey labels and she fixed the spelling.
S0.think: Privately she thinks it changes nothing for her. She'd keep using the tools for her side business and keep doing farm work with her hands.
S0.do: Keeps going at the farm and adds eight more beehives next spring. Grows her honey and egg orders from about 80 to 120 families by Christmas and saves what the side business makes.
S0.quote: It's like asking my nan for advice, except my nan was always right.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is an everyday AI user with a traditional outlook built around family, church and her own small business. Her honey trade is where she feels most herself. She treats the tools as useful helpers, not something to be excited or scared about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to roll their sleeves up and learn the new tools, like farmers always have. I'd say the honey business is proof you can make your own way. I'd post that, maybe a bit smugly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in good shape. I already use the tools, I've got a side business, and I've got a house. The Moreaus will want someone who knows the machines, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to help the Moreaus pick the new kit for the poultry sheds, maybe an egg-collecting robot. I'd bring more AI into the honey orders and add delivery routes. And I'd put some savings into more hives and a proper honey room in the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. A bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think changes at the Moreaus' farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The egg collecting and the shed checks first. There are cameras now that spot a sick bird before you do. That's my morning, but I'd rather be the person who checks what the camera says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think anyone should step in, government or otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Churches and families look after their own round here, and that works better than forms. Maybe some help with training, but run by farmers, not offices in the city.

S1.say: She'd say people need to roll their sleeves up and learn the new tools, like farmers always have. Her honey business shows you can make your own way.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she's in good shape: she uses the tools, has a side business and owns a house. The farm will want someone who knows the machines, and that could be her.
S1.do: Offers to help the farm choose new poultry-shed kit, like an egg-collecting robot. Brings more AI into her honey orders, and puts savings into more hives and a honey room in her garage.
S1.quote: There are cameras now that spot a sick bird before you do.
S1.fieldNote: She combines a traditional preference for self-reliance with early adoption of tools, and sees no conflict between them. She'd steer automation on the farm rather than resist it. Help from government only appeals if farmers run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together like never before. I'd say people should hold on to land and homes, because that's real. I'd say it at church, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be shaken. My job at the Moreaus' goes, probably fast, and if AI can run a honey business, so can anyone. But I've got a house, savings and bees, so I wouldn't be on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast in the first month: put savings into more hives and land for them, and buy any small robots that help me do more on my own. I'd keep the farm job as long as it lasted. I'd ask my brother about turning the house's back paddock into a proper smallholding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Shaken, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What happens to the honey business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets more crowded, I'd guess, with robot honey from big companies. But people round here buy from someone they know. I'd lean on that, the face at the door with the jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Gabor do about your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably marry sooner and stay put. Gabor fixes engines, and robots still break, at least for a while. We'd want to start a family on our own patch, not in someone else's shed.

S2.say: She'd say families and communities will need to pull together like never before. People should hold on to land and homes, because that's real.
S2.think: Privately she'd be shaken: her farm job goes fast, and if AI can run a honey business, so can anyone. But with a house, savings and bees, she wouldn't be on the street.
S2.do: Puts savings into more hives and land in the first month, and buys small robots to do more on her own. Plans a smallholding in the back paddock with her brother and marries sooner.
S2.feel: Uneasy and shaken, but not scared.
S2.quote: People round here buy from someone they know. I'd lean on that, the face at the door with the jar.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario, her house, savings and side business keep her steady. She bets on local trust as the thing machines can't copy. Marriage and family move forward rather than back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. Learn the tools, start something small, keep your family close. I'd say it on my honey page, between the jar photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me fine. That's long enough to turn the honey and eggs into a proper business with the smallholding. By the time it arrives, I'd own the robots, not work beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd go part-time at the Moreaus' and put that time into the smallholding. I'd use AI tools to plan the business and buy a second-hand egg-collecting robot once prices drop. I'd grow to 30 hives and 200 families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Busy and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be grabbing what I can. With five I can plan, borrow sensibly, and do it right. That's a proper difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Dunn at the beekeepers' club. He's 79, knows everything about bees and nothing about computers. I'd want to learn everything from him before the world stops asking him.

S3.say: She'd say five years is plenty for anyone with some get-up-and-go: learn the tools, start something small and keep family close.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years suits her, long enough to turn honey and eggs into a proper business. By the time AGI arrives, she'd own the robots, not work beside them.
S3.do: Goes part-time at the farm in the first year to build her smallholding. Uses AI to plan the business, buys a second-hand egg-collecting robot and grows to 30 hives and 200 families.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, busy and a bit excited.
S3.quote: I'd want to learn everything from him before the world stops asking him.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for her to build a real business, and her mood lifts with it. Her care for the old beekeeper shows her respect for tradition alongside her love of new tools. She frames success as owning the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it waiting for someone to hand you something. Plan, save and build. I'd say it at church and to the young farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine with this. Ten years means I can learn the whole farm properly, build the honey business slowly, and have kids before it all arrives. It's almost too comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working full time at the Moreaus' for a few years, learning everything. Grow the honey business a bit each year and keep saving. Around 2030 I'd go full time on the smallholding, with robots for the hard bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit too comfortable, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Would you still go part-time early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd stay full time a bit longer. The Moreaus have taught me more in two years than school did in ten. I want to learn turkeys from them properly before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, two kids, a smallholding with bees and hens, and a robot that does the heavy lifting. Gabor fixing everyone's machines. Sunday lunch with my brother's lot.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it waiting for someone to hand you something. Plan, save and build.
S4.think: Privately she's fine with it, since ten years lets her learn the whole farm, grow the honey business slowly and have children before it arrives. It feels almost too comfortable.
S4.do: Keeps working full time at the farm for a few years and grows the honey business steadily while saving. Moves full time onto her smallholding around 2030, with robots for the heavy work.
S4.feel: Calm, maybe a bit too comfortable.
S4.quote: The Moreaus have taught me more in two years than school did in ten.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she slows down and puts learning the craft ahead of the business. She notices she might be too comfortable but doesn't seem worried by it. Her picture of 2036 is family-centred, with machines doing the heavy lifting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to grow the honey business properly before everyone else piles in. What would help is less paperwork for small food businesses, so people like me can start up quickly, and cheap loans for land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about trust. Everyone thinks it's about who's cheapest. Round here, people buy honey from the woman whose bees they've seen, and I hope that doesn't change.

headlineQuote: By the time it arrives, I'd own the robots, not work beside them.
portrait: Wendy Varga is a 27-year-old junior worker on the Moreau family's poultry, sheep and arable farm, living with her boyfriend Gabor, a mechanic, in a house she inherited with her brother. She keeps bees and sells honey and eggs to local families through an order site she built with AI, which she uses every day. She's traditional, puts family, church and self-reliance first, and wants to own the machines rather than compete with them. Only the two-year AGI picture shakes her, and even then her house, savings and local customers keep her steady.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to grow the honey business before everyone else piled in.
whatWouldHelp: Less paperwork for small food businesses so people can start up quickly, and cheap loans for land.
